## [2026-10-28](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-28.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Advancement or Acceleration? How Data Curation Improves LLM Training](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36983>)

This study separates data curation that reaches an existing solution sooner from curation that improves attainable target performance, and tests a baseline training-target loss-gap diagnostic. Controlled small-model experiments show why target alignment and training budget should be examined before interpreting a fixed-budget gain as a lasting capability improvement.

**Published:** 2026-10-27 · **First seen:** 2026-10-28T10:02:23.983Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Data Curation, Target Distribution, Training Budgets, Scaling Diagnostics

**Public availability:** 2026-10-28T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.LG/new?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2610.36983v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Main methods/results and relevant appendices inspected. Five-run SlimPajama experiments at 160M show near-matched-target perplexities 19.71 for Uniform and 19.66 for TANDEM, versus 28.60/26.02 with repeated scarce-domain data; 1.1B tests retain the contrast. Selection separately varies target distributions. Delta is measured halfway through baseline training. Original October 28 cs.LG batch and official Tuesday schedule imply 00:00 UTC announcement. Author code remains pending internal approval.

**Limitations:** The endpoint theorem assumes global population-risk minimization; finite LLM budgets do not verify infinite-budget optimality. Delta compares seen-training and target losses, not distributions, so equal losses can hide mismatch. Selection uses target-aware reference data and unequal retained tokens versus full-pool training. Models stop at 1.1B; no complete end-to-end curation-cost benefit was demonstrated.

## [2026-10-18](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-18.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [No Single Tokenizer Feature Reliably Predicts Downstream Language Model Performance](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21679>)

Across three small-model suites and nine languages, this study finds that popular tokenizer metrics correlate inconsistently with downstream quality, even when individual task correlations appear strong. The results support validating tokenizer choices on representative tasks and languages instead of treating compression or a single intrinsic score as a reliable accuracy proxy.

**Published:** 2026-10-15 · **First seen:** 2026-10-17T10:02:15.889Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Tokenizer Evaluation, Multilingual Models, Intrinsic Metrics

**Public availability:** 2026-10-16T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.CL/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21679>) · [Code](<https://github.com/shikhar-srivastava/vista-training>) · [Project](<https://huggingface.co/collections/shikhar-srivastava/vista-130m>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Full Sections 3–10 and the model, evaluation, statistical and robustness appendices inspected again. Three suites cover 14 TokSuite 1B models, 45 usable TIMTC 350M models after nine OOV exclusions, and multilingual VISTA 130M/350M models; 29 intrinsic metrics and 48 distinct benchmark tasks span nine languages. The analysis z-scores accuracy within language and task, corrects multiple comparisons, controls parameter counts and repeats the analysis after excluding near-chance cases. The strongest aggregate correlations are only r=0.27, 0.24 and 0.22, while signs and rankings change across tasks, languages and suites. A metric explains at most an additional 0.021 R-squared beyond model size; pairs of intrinsic metrics reach at most 0.09 joint R-squared. Existing VISTA training code and model collections were verified both in the prior run and today. This was a reviewed but unpublished reserve on October 17, below that run’s selected contributions; fresh reassessment now includes its useful tokenizer-selection lesson within the remaining 72-hour lookback. Its original October 17 first-seen time is preserved. No indexing delay is claimed.

**Limitations:** These observational correlations do not show that tokenizers do not matter or that a better metric cannot exist. Models are at most 1B parameters, some tasks are near chance, language coverage and suite training budgets differ, vocabulary sizes change embedding parameter counts, and annotated intrinsic resources are uneven across languages. Compression can still reduce cost without predicting accuracy. The VISTA link is training code, not the complete current paper-analysis pipeline. The main analysis repository, unavailable with 404 responses during the prior run, loaded today, but its sole observed code commit is October 18 at 21:13Z, after the report’s 10:00Z cutoff. That later artifact is not used as an in-window contribution or advertised as available by the cutoff; its exact first public visibility is not inferred from Git metadata. An undated author homepage lists the title without a paper link and does not establish an earlier full-method release.

## [2026-10-13](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-13.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [MagicBeanStalk: Escaping the RLVR Zero Advantage Trap with Recursive Data Synthesis](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12659>)

MagicBeanStalk decomposes hard problems into verified subproblems, then recombines new variants into training tasks calibrated to a target model and response budget. It turns otherwise uninformative all-failure reward groups into useful reinforcement-learning data while preserving the reasoning skills that made the original seeds valuable.

**Published:** 2026-10-08 · **First seen:** 2026-10-15T04:36:31.851Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Synthetic Data, RLVR, Difficulty Calibration

**Public availability:** 2026-10-12T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.AI/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12659>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Delayed discovery of the October 12 new-submission batch; availability is inferred from that dated primary-category batch and the official schedule. Sections 2–4 and Appendices D–G provide synthesis controls, qualification screens and evaluations; gpt-oss-120b improves from 61.2 to 69.8 average pass@1 across eight math benchmarks at 16K output tokens.

**Limitations:** Difficulty is a finite-sample, policy-and-budget-dependent estimate. Synthesis and some verification rely on proprietary teachers; data release is promised upon acceptance. Extra synthesis cost is not an end-to-end efficiency win. Synthetic errors and unequal sample counts limit cross-model comparisons; no results were independently reproduced.

## [2026-10-11](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-11.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Language-Specific Effects of Tokenizer Choice in Multilingual Language Models](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12144>)

A controlled multilingual study measures how tokenizer choices affect individual languages and tests inexpensive metrics for screening candidates before model training. The results favor language-specific evaluation over a single average and show why allocating more tokenizer capacity to a low-resource language should be validated rather than assumed beneficial.

**Published:** 2026-10-08 · **First seen:** 2026-10-11T10:02:36Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Tokenization, Multilingual, Controlled Ablations

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12144>) · [Project](<https://huggingface.co/cmeister/tokenizer-lm-ablations>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Sections 2–6 compare 123 models spanning 54 tokenizers; the main setup uses 1.27B models and 9.2B tokens. Family-held-out ranking reaches 89.0% accuracy for mean FLORES+ bits-per-byte. Newly discovered October 8 paper, announced in October 9's batch; the linked artifact predates this analysis, so no earliest-public timestamp or new-weight release is asserted.

**Limitations:** Mostly one seed per tokenizer, one main architecture/vocabulary scale and observational metric correlations. Fixed tokens change training bytes; task-level generalization remains limited. GitHub and artifact history were inaccessible, and exact artifact parity is unverified.

## [2026-10-09](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-09.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Adapting English Quality Classifiers for Multilingual LLM Pretraining Data Selection](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11585>)

This pipeline transfers English data-quality criteria to multilingual text by scoring translations and training small classifiers over frozen multilingual embeddings. Released classifiers achieve broadly comparable downstream performance to strong multilingual filters, making quality selection easier to extend without collecting separate annotations for every language.

**Published:** 2026-10-08 · **First seen:** 2026-10-09T10:03:31Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Data Curation, Multilingual, Quality Filtering

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. The study tests 1B training from scratch and 3B/8B cooldown runs, selecting the top 10% of documents per language. Regional and cultural checks accompany classifier-transfer analyses, and the author model card exposes weights and inference code. Original v1: 2026-10-08T09:33:32Z; October 9 new-submission batch verified. Conservatively marked newly discovered: the confirmed paper batch is recent, but the earlier public availability of its classifier artifact cannot be reconstructed.

**Limitations:** The largest models receive short cooldowns, not complete matched pretraining. Long-tail evidence partly uses synthetic text and LLM judges, and limited cultural benchmarks cannot establish absence of bias. Translation cost and inherited English quality preferences remain; prior public artifact timing is uncertain after repository-history squashing.

## [2026-10-05](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-05.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [LESSER: Post-Training Data Selection with Output-Layer Gradients](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03702>)

LESSER selects post-training data using output-layer gradient features computed from a forward pass, replacing expensive backpropagation-based gradient extraction while retaining existing selection rules. Across supervised fine-tuning, RL data selection, and teacher selection, these cheaper features largely preserve the tested selectors' quality, making targeted training-data curation more practical.

**Published:** 2026-10-02 · **First seen:** 2026-10-05T10:03:24Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Data Selection, Gradient Features, Post-Training

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03702>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. The SFT study covers four models, five tasks, three subset sizes, and three seeds; the mean absolute gap from LESS is 1.3 points. Reported SFT feature-extraction FLOPs fall 9.7-fold. Submission: 2026-10-02T17:55:42Z; the October 5 cs.LG batch confirms public announcement on October 5 at 00:00Z under arXiv's schedule.

**Limitations:** The SFT comparison also changes checkpoint preparation: LESS uses four warmup checkpoints whereas LESSER uses the base model, so it does not isolate only the feature representation. The method requires target-query data. Savings concern selection features, not total training; the reported SFT wall-clock estimate is extrapolated. No author implementation URL was verified.

## [2026-10-02](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-02.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Universal Byte-Level Encoding: UTF-8/UTF-16 Routing to Reduce Cross-Script Token-Budget Disparities](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01984>)

Universal Byte-Level Encoding routes characters between UTF-8 and UTF-16 before standard byte-pair encoding, reducing the initial encoding cost for several scripts while preserving exact decoding. It can reduce multilingual token-budget disparities and fit more content into a fixed context window, particularly with compact vocabularies and poorly covered scripts.

**Published:** 2026-10-01 · **First seen:** 2026-10-02T15:32:39Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Tokenization, Multilingual Models, Data Efficiency

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01984>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Matched tokenizer-data comparisons span 204 language-script configurations, Unicode round-trip audits, and language models from 182M to 1.3B. The 101-language/32K setting reduces token-premium Gini by 9.4%; language-model quality differences are small and mixed. arXiv v1: 2026-10-01T16:26:10Z, within this report's interval. The timestamp above is submission time; the arXiv cs.CL listing separately confirms the October 2 public announcement batch.

**Limitations:** Changing vocabulary requires retraining or adaptation rather than swapping into an existing checkpoint. Some languages regress, the largest token savings include scripts outside the downstream training corpus, and three-seed results do not establish improved language-model loss parity.

## [2026-10-02](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-02.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Scalable, Transferable Meta-network for Data Selection Requires a Different Loss (and Why the Obvious Choice is Problematic)](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02092>)

TESS learns a reusable data-selection network by matching per-example loss differences between ordinary and validation-guided models, avoiding a weighting objective that can suppress most examples and favor shortcuts. It transfers selection from a smaller sample to unseen instruction data, offering a way to target fine-tuning data without relearning a separate weight for every example.

**Published:** 2026-10-01 · **First seen:** 2026-10-02T15:32:39Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Data Selection, Meta-Learning, Instruction Tuning

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02092>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. A selector trained on 50K Tulu V2 examples is applied to 197K candidates before Llama-2-7B fine-tuning; math/code task-average performance is 26.46 versus 21.54 for random selection. Loss ablations and cross-dataset probes support transfer. arXiv v1: 2026-10-01T17:23:29Z. The timestamp above is submission time; the arXiv cs.CL listing separately confirms the October 2 public announcement batch.

**Limitations:** Task-specific validation examples and representation/gradient features are required. Evidence uses a limited set of older model families and tasks; the safety experiment measures harmful-data identification, not improved safety. Code release is promised upon acceptance rather than verified as available.

## [2026-09-29 — Landscape baseline](../../../landscape/2026-09-29.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [It's All Training: A Fully Synthetic Single-Stage Recipe for LLMs](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37891>)

SYNTH turns curated Wikipedia seeds into grounded questions, reasoning traces, and varied tasks, allowing small language models to acquire instruction-following behavior within a single training stage. Controlled data ablations make it a useful reference for testing whether carefully generated synthetic data can improve learning efficiency and targeted factual recall.

**Published:** 2026-09-29 · **First seen:** 2026-09-30T03:57:00Z · **Novelty:** baseline · **Tags:** Synthetic Data, Pretraining, Small Models

**Positioning:** frontier-research

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37891>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Sections 3-5 describe generation and matched 600M-model data ablations; the authors report an 11-17 point advantage over their post-trained web-data controls across the aggregate task groups.

**Limitations:** Knowledge is bounded by roughly 58,000 seed articles, language coverage is shaped by English sources, and experiments target small models; token savings are not equivalent to total savings once teacher generation is counted.
